name: SiteOne Crawler
purpose: PHP-based crawler that inventories a website's structure, assets, third-party components, security headers and performance characteristics, and can export an offline copy or a sitemap.
journalism_use_case: Inventory a target site's structure, assets and third-party components, and keep an offline copy for reference — the third-party-component inventory is the investigative hook, since it reveals which trackers, analytics and foreign services a government or company site loads.
pros: Third-party component inventory is directly useful for the surveillance-adjacent story: which analytics, tracking and data-processing services a public-sector site embeds
Produces a readable report rather than raw data, so a non-engineer can act on the findings
MIT licensed, single-command operation, with a current release (v2.5.1, 2026-06-27) and a small backlog
Covers security headers and performance alongside structure, giving a broad picture in one pass
cons: Analysis and export focus rather than archival WARC output, so it is not an evidence-capture tool
Vendor-led project (SiteOne) with a commercial website behind it, so direction follows the vendor's interests — not a problem for the MIT code, but a continuity consideration
PHP toolchain is an odd fit for most newsroom stacks
Last push 2026-09-27 with the release three months earlier; modest community (1,015 stars) means limited third-party knowledge to draw on
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 1,015 stars with 17 open issues, release v2.5.1 (2026-06-27), latest tag v2.6.1, last push 2026-09-27, MIT licence.
assessment: Worth running once against sites you are investigating, specifically for the third-party component list — that single output can seed a story about what a ministry's website sends to whom. For tracker analysis specifically, Blacklight and Exodus Privacy give you a stronger, journalism-oriented account. I would treat SiteOne as a general reconnaissance report rather than a core tool, and not build a pipeline on it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-27, latest release v2.5.1 (2026-06-27), latest tag v2.6.1, 1,015 stars, 17 open issues. Two months since last push with a tag ahead of the release; steady vendor-led maintenance at modest velocity.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute; disk for offline copies.
privacy: Direct crawl of the target with reports written locally; nothing uploaded. The target sees your crawl.
alternatives: Blacklight (the-markup/blacklight-collector) for journalism-oriented tracker analysis
Exodus Privacy for the mobile-app equivalent
katana plus manual review for structure enumeration

name: Photon
purpose: Fast Python crawler that harvests URLs, email addresses, social handles, document links, subdomains and JavaScript files from a target site in a single pass.
journalism_use_case: Harvest contact details, document links and handles scattered across a target website in one pass — useful for building a contact list for a company under investigation, or for finding the PDFs buried in an agency site.
pros: Single-pass extraction of several artefact types (emails, handles, documents, subdomains) is efficient for reconnaissance, where you otherwise run four tools
Optionally queries the Internet Archive CDX, so it finds URLs that no longer exist on the live site — a genuinely useful investigative addition
Lightweight pure-Python with no heavy dependencies, so it runs anywhere
Large user base (13,350 stars) and a readable codebase
cons: Light maintenance cadence relative to its age: the last release v1.3.0 dates from 2019-04-05, with the last push 2026-10-17 — commits continue but release engineering stopped years ago
No JavaScript rendering, so modern dynamic sites yield little
Harvesting email addresses and handles creates a personal-data collection with attendant data-protection obligations that reporters rarely consider
61 open issues; security-tooling heritage means defaults are not tuned for politeness
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 13,350 stars with 61 open issues, release v1.3.0 (2019-04-05), last push 2026-10-17. The seven-year gap between the last release and current commits is the notable signal.
assessment: Still useful for its specific harvesting job, with two cautions for your work. First, the lack of releases means pinning to a commit rather than a version. Second and more important: the output is a personal-data set (emails, names, handles), so treat it as regulated material with a retention decision, not as a scratch file — that is a discipline most OSINT tooling ignores and that a newsroom cannot. Pair with katana for completeness on dynamic sites.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-17, latest release v1.3.0 (2019-04-05), 13,350 stars, 61 open issues. Commits within the last month but no release in seven years — a maintained-but-unreleased pattern. Classified stable-low rather than declining because activity is current.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 limits embedding in proprietary tooling. Note that harvested personal data carries data-protection obligations independent of the licence.
privacy: Crawls the target directly with results written to local JSON/text, so the target sees your requests. The more significant privacy issue is on your side: you are creating a collection of other people's contact details, which needs a retention and protection decision.
alternatives: katana for more thorough modern URL discovery
theHarvester for email and host harvesting from public sources rather than a site crawl
Manual review for small targets, avoiding the personal-data collection entirely

name: Hyphe
purpose: Research web crawler that builds a curated corpus of websites with human decisions about inclusion, aggregating pages into 'web entities' and producing a link network between them.
journalism_use_case: Map an ecosystem — a disinformation network, a lobbying cluster, a set of linked front organisations — by curating which sites belong to the corpus and visualising how they link. The curation step is what makes the resulting network defensible rather than an artefact of crawler scope.
pros: Human-in-the-loop corpus curation is the methodological point: the researcher decides what counts as an entity, so the resulting network reflects a defensible definition rather than crawler accident
Aggregating many URLs into web entities matches how investigations think (an organisation, not a hostname), which is unusual and valuable
Produces a link network directly exportable to Gephi for analysis and publication
Built by a social-science methods lab with a long record in network mapping, so the data model is designed for this analysis
cons: Heavy install (Docker, MongoDB, ScrapyD components) and six months since the last push (2026-05-18) with the last release in July 2025 — slowing cadence for a complex multi-service system
Curation is manual and labour-intensive: a meaningful corpus takes days of analyst attention, which is the real cost and the reason projects stall
Link networks invite over-interpretation — a hyperlink is not a relationship, and published network graphs are routinely read as proving coordination
Small community (392 stars) and research-oriented documentation
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 392 stars with 56 open issues, release v1.12.2 (2025-07-07), last push 2026-05-18. médialab tools are used in academic and journalistic network research, which is credible adjacent context.
assessment: The right instrument when the story is the shape of a network and you can commit analyst time to curation. For your profile I would pilot it on a bounded question (for example, which sites link to a known disinformation outlet and how they cluster) rather than as standing infrastructure, given the install weight and slowing cadence. Be disciplined in publication: state the inclusion criteria, and never present a hyperlink graph as evidence of coordination without corroborating evidence.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-05-18, latest release v1.12.2 (2025-07-07), 392 stars, 56 open issues. Six months without commits and sixteen months since the last release, on a multi-service system with a Docker/MongoDB dependency surface that ages. Declining rather than dormant; no deprecation notice.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Crawled content belongs to the original publishers.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0 network copyleft if you modify and expose an instance. Internal use unaffected.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a Docker host with MongoDB and crawler components — one reasonably sized VM for a modest corpus. The dominant cost is analyst curation time, realistically days per corpus. Assumptions: self-hosted, single-analyst workflow.
privacy: Crawled pages and the link graph are stored in your own instance. Your crawler is visible to the target sites, which for a disinformation-network investigation means the targets can see they are being crawled — consider a dedicated egress.
alternatives: minet plus Gephi for a lighter scripted approach to the same network question
Gephi alone if you already have the link data
4CAT for platform-centric rather than website-centric network mapping

name: Heritrix 3
purpose: The Internet Archive's production archival crawler: a Java system for large-scale, politeness-respecting WARC crawls with fine-grained scope control and a web operator interface.
journalism_use_case: Large-scale archival crawls of whole domains where the capture must be WARC-based and defensible — for example preserving an entire ministry site, with request and response headers intact, before an anticipated purge.
pros: WARC output with full request/response fidelity is the evidentiary gold standard, and Heritrix is the reference implementation used by national libraries and the Internet Archive itself
Scope control and politeness configuration are unmatched, which matters when crawling a large public-sector domain you must not degrade
Actively maintained (release 3.18.0, 2026-10-06; pushed 2026-11-17) with a small backlog for a project of this size (44 open issues)
Institutional provenance means your capture methodology can be described in terms an archivist or a court would recognise
cons: Steep learning curve: the Spring-based configuration model and the operator UI are unlike anything else in this catalogue, and a first successful crawl takes real effort
Weak on dynamic and JavaScript-dependent content — it captures what a non-executing fetcher sees, so modern single-page portals come out hollow; browsertrix-crawler is the right tool there
Java plus substantial storage, and WARC collections need an index (OutbackCDX) and a replay front end (pywb) before anyone can read them — the full stack is three components
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION despite Apache-2.0, so licence records need the file reference
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. The institutional usage evidence is strong and verifiable: Heritrix is the Internet Archive's own crawler and is used across the IIPC web-archiving community. 3,351 stars, 44 open issues, release 3.18.0 (2026-10-06).
assessment: The right choice for domain-scale archival capture where defensibility matters, and over-engineered for anything smaller. For your profile I would reserve it for a planned preservation project — an at-risk government domain, a complete site before litigation — and use browsertrix-crawler for social and dynamic material. Budget for the whole stack: Heritrix to crawl, OutbackCDX to index, pywb to serve, or the collection is unusable by reporters.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 3.18.0 (2026-10-06), SPDX NOASSERTION (Apache-2.0 per repository), 3,351 stars, 44 open issues. Current releases and commits under Internet Archive stewardship with a web-archiving community behind it.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Captured content belongs to the original publishers.
licence_restrictions: None material. Confirm the licence file reference for compliance records given the SPDX gap.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a JVM host plus substantial storage — WARC collections are large (expect the raw site size plus overhead), and a domain crawl can be hundreds of GB. Add storage for the CDX index. Assumptions: self-hosted, single-domain crawls.
privacy: WARCs are written to your own storage. Your crawler is visible to the target, and a Heritrix crawl is identifiable by its user agent — configure it honestly, since misrepresenting a crawler is both an ethical and potentially legal problem.
alternatives: browsertrix-crawler for high-fidelity capture of dynamic and social content
wget --warc for small WARC captures without the operational overhead
grab-site for steerable rapid-response crawls — with its maintenance caveat

name: brozzler
purpose: Distributed crawler that drives real Chrome instances, proxying all traffic through warcprox to produce WARCs, with RethinkDB coordinating jobs across workers.
journalism_use_case: Archive JavaScript-dependent pages at scale where a plain crawler would capture empty shells — for example a dynamic procurement portal or a mapping application whose content only exists after script execution.
pros: Browser-based capture through a recording proxy gives both fidelity (the page as rendered) and WARC provenance (the actual HTTP exchanges) — the combination that makes dynamic captures evidentiary
Distributed worker model scales to large jobs, unlike single-browser capture tools
Apache-2.0 and actively released (v1.10.0, 2026-11-14, same-day push) under Internet Archive stewardship
Pairs with warcprox, which the same organisation maintains, so the components are coherent
cons: Operationally complex multi-service deployment: Chrome instances, warcprox, RethinkDB and workers — the heaviest capture stack here, and RethinkDB in particular is an unusual dependency with its own maintenance history
Internet Archive internal priorities drive development, so feature direction may not match a newsroom's needs
63 open issues and documentation aimed at operators already familiar with the IA stack
Browser-based crawling is resource-hungry: capture throughput per machine is far below a static crawler's
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 824 stars with 63 open issues, release v1.10.0 on 2026-11-14 with same-day push. Used in production by the Internet Archive, which is verifiable from the organisation's tooling and is the strongest provenance available.
assessment: Capable but hard to justify for a newsroom when browsertrix-crawler delivers comparable browser-based WARC/WACZ capture with a far simpler Docker deployment. I would choose brozzler only if you are already operating in an Internet-Archive-aligned stack or need its distributed worker model for very large dynamic crawls. For your profile, browsertrix-crawler is the pragmatic default and this is the fallback at scale.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v1.10.0 published the same day, 824 stars, 63 open issues. Current releases under institutional maintenance with production use at the Internet Archive.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: multiple worker machines running Chrome plus warcprox and a RethinkDB instance — materially more expensive per captured page than static crawling. Assumptions: self-hosted, moderate crawl volume.
privacy: Captured traffic is proxied through warcprox into WARC files you hold. Note that proxying everything means credentials and session tokens used during capture are written into the WARC — treat the output as sensitive.
alternatives: browsertrix-crawler — recommended: same capability class, much simpler deployment
Heritrix for static domain-scale crawling
ArchiveWeb.page for manual capture of individual dynamic pages

name: grab-site
purpose: Archival crawler built on wpull that produces WARCs with a live dashboard, allowing the operator to add ignore patterns and adjust scope while the crawl is running.
journalism_use_case: Rapid-response archiving of a site at risk of deletion, with the ability to steer the crawl while it runs — which matters when you have minutes rather than hours and need to avoid wasting the window on a calendar or a session-ID trap.
pros: Live steering during a crawl is the distinguishing feature and genuinely valuable under time pressure: you can see the crawl falling into a trap and exclude it without restarting
WARC output, so captures are evidentiary rather than loose files
Developed by ArchiveTeam, whose entire purpose is rapid preservation of at-risk sites, so the design priorities match the emergency use case
Large community for a specialist tool (1,617 stars)
cons: Eighteen months since the last push (2025-05-23) and it depends on wpull, which was itself last pushed in April 2024 — a dormant dependency under a slowing project is a compounding risk
103 open issues and no release objects (latest tag 2.2.7), so there is no supported version to pin
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION despite MIT, so licence records need the file reference
Python dependency chain of this age is increasingly awkward to install on current systems
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: last push 2025-05-23, 1,617 stars, 103 open issues, no releases, SPDX NOASSERTION; its dependency wpull was last pushed 2024-04-29 (verified separately in this catalogue). The dependency's dormancy is the more serious signal.
assessment: The steering capability is worth knowing about, but I would not make it the rapid-response tool of record given the dormant wpull dependency. For your profile the more reliable emergency path is browsertrix-crawler with a prepared configuration, or `wget --warc` for a quick WARC with no setup — both maintained. If you do keep grab-site, containerise it now while it still installs, because the Python chain will get harder.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-05-23, no release objects, latest tag 2.2.7, SPDX NOASSERTION, 1,617 stars, 103 open issues. Eighteen months without commits, and its core dependency wpull last pushed 2024-04-29. Both layers stalled, so dormant rather than merely low-activity.
licence_restrictions: None material; confirm the licence file for records.
costs: No fee. Disk for WARCs. Hidden cost is install effort on a current system.
privacy: WARC and logs are written locally; nothing is uploaded. The target sees your crawl.
alternatives: browsertrix-crawler with a prepared config for maintained rapid capture
wget --warc for an immediate, dependency-free WARC
ArchiveBot to mobilise community capacity for a very large at-risk site
blockers: Dormant since May 2025; depends on wpull, dormant since April 2024

name: wpull
purpose: Python reimplementation of wget with WARC output, wget-compatible flags, a plugin/hook system and database-backed crawl state.
journalism_use_case: Wget-style recursive capture when you need WARC output and wget's familiar flag semantics — historically the engine beneath grab-site and a bridge for anyone who already thinks in wget options.
pros: wget-compatible flags lower the learning curve substantially for anyone who already uses wget, while adding proper WARC output
Database-backed crawl state makes large crawls resumable, which plain wget does not do well
Plugin hooks allow custom scope logic, which is how grab-site implemented live steering
GPL-3.0 with a sizeable historical community (613 stars)
cons: Effectively dormant: last push 2024-04-29, no release objects (latest tag v2.0.3), and 208 open issues — the largest backlog-to-stars ratio in this subcategory
Its dormancy propagates: grab-site depends on it, so two tools stall together
Python dependency chain of this vintage is increasingly difficult to install on current interpreters
Modern wget itself supports --warc, removing much of wpull's original rationale
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: last push 2024-04-29, 613 stars, 208 open issues, no releases, latest tag v2.0.3. The large unattended backlog alongside no commits for over two years is unambiguous.
assessment: Avoid for new work. `wget --warc` covers the simple case with a maintained binary, and browsertrix-crawler covers the fidelity case. The only reason to touch wpull now is to understand or repair grab-site. For your profile, note the general pattern worth applying across this catalogue: when a tool's sole differentiator has been absorbed into a maintained upstream (here, wget's WARC support), the tool's dormancy is terminal rather than temporary.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-04-29, no release objects, latest tag v2.0.3, 613 stars, 208 open issues. Over two and a half years without commits and a very large open backlog. No deprecation notice, hence dormant rather than archived.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0; immaterial given the recommendation not to use it.
costs: No fee. Install effort on current Python is the real cost.
alternatives: wget --warc — maintained, simple, covers the core case
browsertrix-crawler for dynamic content with WACZ output
Heritrix for domain-scale archival crawls
blockers: Dormant since April 2024 with a 208-issue backlog; superseded by wget's own WARC support

name: ArchiveBot
purpose: IRC-driven distributed archiving system where volunteers request crawls of at-risk sites, which are executed across ArchiveTeam's pipeline fleet and ingested into Internet Archive collections.
journalism_use_case: Mobilise community archiving capacity when a large site must be preserved faster than one newsroom can manage — for example a government portal announced for shutdown, where thousands of pages must be captured in days.
pros: Access to capacity no newsroom has: ArchiveTeam's pipeline fleet can crawl at a scale and speed a single organisation cannot match
Captures land in public ArchiveTeam/Internet Archive collections, so the preservation is durable and third-party attested rather than sitting on your disk
Mature, long-running community infrastructure still receiving commits (pushed 2026-09-08)
Costs you nothing but a request
cons: Not a private tool: you are requesting work from a community, with public IRC logs, so your interest in a specific site becomes public immediately — disqualifying when the target should not know
Captures are ingested into public collections, so you cannot use it for material you intend to hold confidentially
No control over timing or completeness: the community decides what gets crawled and how
194 open issues against 429 stars, and operating your own instance is impractical — this is a service you ask for, not software you run
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 429 stars with 194 open issues, last push 2026-09-08, MIT licence. ArchiveTeam's track record in rescuing at-risk sites is extensively documented on its own wiki, which is the relevant context for whether a request is likely to be actioned.
assessment: A genuinely useful escalation route for public-interest preservation at scale, with one hard constraint you must internalise: requesting a crawl is a public act. For your profile the decision rule is clean — if the target knowing you are interested is harmless or even helpful (an announced shutdown of a public dataset), use ArchiveBot; if it would compromise an investigation, capture it yourself with browsertrix-crawler and accept the smaller scale.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-08, no releases, 429 stars, 194 open issues. Two months since last push on long-lived community infrastructure; the large backlog is characteristic of volunteer-operated systems. The operational service rather than the repository is the artefact.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Captures enter public Internet Archive collections under their terms.
licence_restrictions: None material for the code. The operational consequence is the point: captures become public.
costs: Free. You are using donated community capacity, which carries an etiquette obligation rather than a monetary one.
privacy: Not private: requests are made over a public IRC channel with public logs, and captures are ingested into public ArchiveTeam/Internet Archive collections. Treat any request as a public disclosure of your interest.
alternatives: browsertrix-crawler or Heritrix for private capture under your own control
ArchiveBox for a private self-hosted archive
Direct Internet Archive 'Save Page Now' for individual pages
blockers: Requests and captures are public — unusable for confidential investigation

name: pywb
purpose: Python web-archiving toolkit providing high-fidelity replay of WARC and WACZ collections, a recording proxy mode, collection management and a Wayback-style interface.
journalism_use_case: Stand up a private Wayback Machine over your own captures so editors and lawyers can click through dated versions of a government page side by side without relying on a public archive staying online — the piece that turns a WARC collection from a pile of files into usable evidence.
pros: Turns inert WARC files into something a non-technical colleague can actually use, which is the difference between having evidence and being able to show it
High replay fidelity by the standards of the field, maintained by the team that drives much of modern web-archiving practice
Very actively maintained (v2.11.1 released 2026-11-14, pushed 2026-11-17) with a substantial community (1,720 stars)
Also works as a recording proxy, so it can capture as well as replay — useful for a single integrated setup
cons: Replay and recording only: no change detection, diffing or alerting, so it is one component of a monitoring or evidence system rather than a solution
Replay fidelity for heavily scripted modern pages remains an open problem in web archiving generally — pywb does as well as anything, which is not the same as perfectly
GPL-3.0 copyleft is a consideration if you embed replay in a product you distribute
185 open issues and a configuration surface that takes learning; what it exposes to the network depends entirely on how you deploy it
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,720 stars with 185 open issues, release v-2.11.1 (2026-11-14), pushed 2026-11-17. pywb is used across the web-archiving community including by institutional archives, verifiable from IIPC community documentation.
assessment: Adopt it as the replay layer for any serious capture programme — without replay, WARCs are write-only. For your profile the deployment decision that matters is access control: a pywb instance over an investigation's captures is a high-value target and must not be publicly reachable. Pair with OutbackCDX if the collection grows large enough that URL/timestamp lookup becomes slow.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v-2.11.1 (2026-11-14), 1,720 stars, 185 open issues. Current releases and same-day commits from an organisation whose core business this is.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Replayed content belongs to the original publishers.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0: distributing a modified pywb-based product triggers source-release obligations. Internal deployment is unaffected.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a small Python service plus storage for your WARC/WACZ collection — storage dominates and scales with capture volume. Operating effort is modest once configured.
privacy: Serves local archive files; what it exposes to the network depends entirely on your deployment. A misconfigured public instance would publish your entire capture collection, including anything sensitive you captured — bind it internally and authenticate.
alternatives: ReplayWeb.page for single-file client-side replay with no server at all
Browsertrix (the platform) if you want capture, storage and replay managed together
OutbackCDX plus pywb for large collections needing fast URL indexing
